name: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A
aliases: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type IA

clinicalPearls: The most common inherited neuropathy, accounting for the majority of demyelinating CMT (CMT1) and a large share of all CMT.
Caused by a tandem duplication of PMP22 on chromosome 17, acting through a gene-dosage effect; inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance.

Nerve conduction studies show uniform, symmetrical slowing of motor conduction velocities across all nerves in the demyelinating range, a key feature distinguishing it from acquired demyelinating neuropathies.
Typical onset is within the first two decades, with distal leg weakness, foot drop, pes cavus and hammer toes; hand involvement follows later.
Distal wasting produces the classic inverted-champagne-bottle (stork) leg appearance, with early loss of ankle reflexes and glove-and-stocking sensory loss.
Peripheral nerves may be palpably enlarged owing to onion-bulb hypertrophy from repeated demyelination and remyelination.
Diagnosis is confirmed by targeted PMP22 copy-number testing (for example MLPA) as a first-line test rather than a broad sequencing panel.
Certain neurotoxic drugs, notably vincristine, can precipitate severe, sometimes irreversible deterioration and should be avoided or used with extreme caution.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A results from a tandem duplication of a region on the short arm of chromosome 17 containing PMP22, which encodes peripheral myelin protein 22, a component of compact myelin in the peripheral nervous system. The additional gene copy produces a dosage effect, and overexpression of the protein disrupts Schwann cell function and myelin maintenance. This drives repeated cycles of segmental demyelination and remyelination, generating concentric Schwann cell proliferation (onion bulbs) and hypertrophic nerves, with uniform slowing of conduction along all nerves. Although the primary lesion is in myelin, progressive length-dependent axonal degeneration develops secondarily and is the principal determinant of long-term weakness and disability. Penetrance is high, but severity varies within and between families.
additionalDifferentials: X-linked CMT (GJB1), which shows intermediate, often asymmetric slowing
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (a treatable acquired mimic)
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (PMP22 deletion)
Dejerine-Sottas / congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy at the severe end
additionalInvestigations: Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies demonstrating uniform demyelinating slowing
PMP22 copy-number analysis (MLPA or equivalent duplication testing)
Broader CMT gene panel if the PMP22 duplication is absent
Nerve ultrasound showing diffuse, symmetrical nerve enlargement
Clinical genetic counselling with family segregation studies
Sural nerve biopsy reserved for atypical cases (onion-bulb hypertrophy)
Orthopaedic assessment and foot radiographs for structural deformity
redFlags: Rapid, stepwise or markedly asymmetric progression suggesting superimposed inflammatory neuropathy
Prominent early sensory ataxia, bulbar or respiratory involvement, which is atypical
Severe infantile onset raising suspicion of a PMP22 point mutation or Dejerine-Sottas phenotype
Acute deterioration after exposure to neurotoxic chemotherapy such as vincristine
reference.prognosis: The condition is slowly progressive over decades, and most patients remain ambulant, though many eventually require ankle-foot orthoses. Lifespan is normal.
pitfalls: Attributing all conduction slowing to CMT1A and missing a superimposed, treatable inflammatory neuropathy.
Ordering large sequencing panels before the simple, high-yield PMP22 duplication test.
Administering neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine without recognising the diagnosis.
Assuming normal conduction velocities exclude the disease, when uniform slowing is the hallmark.
Overlooking mildly affected or asymptomatic gene carriers within the family.
management: Manage supportively with physiotherapy and occupational therapy, as there is no disease-modifying drug therapy
Fit ankle-foot orthoses and provide podiatry, appropriate footwear and walking aids for foot drop and pes cavus
Offer orthopaedic foot surgery such as tendon transfer, osteotomy or arthrodesis for fixed, disabling deformity
Treat neuropathic pain and cramps symptomatically and address fatigue
Avoid drugs recognised as neurotoxic, particularly vincristine, which can cause severe deterioration in this subtype
Monitor for scoliosis and, less commonly, respiratory involvement
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant, highly penetrant inheritance and family segregation testing for the PMP22 duplication
Coordinate multidisciplinary neuromuscular, orthopaedic and rehabilitation care
